newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower after profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower after profit-taking.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market ended lower on Friday as profit-taking ended a four-day winning streak.

"The market's had a long run," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Yields got to levels that are near the bottom of the range that we've been in for a long time -- so it's understandable."
The 6-3/4 percent bellwether 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-1/32, down 8/32, to yield 6.91 percent, versus 6.89 percent at Thursday's close.
Building on gains of the four previous sessions, prices rose early in the day, the 30-year bond climbing half a point.

But traders said some late-morning central bank selling in the 10-year sector and hedging related to a large issue of corporate debt by Ford Motor helped to erase the gains. By midday, the 30-year bond had edged into negative territory.

The menu of new economic data was fairly skimpy on Friday. The government revised second-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) down to 4.7 percent from 4.8 percent. And the University of Michigan consumer sentiment final index for September slipped to 94.7 from to 95.3 in the final August index.

Another consideration that could have helped brake the market's advance is the September employment data due on October 4. Also next week, the market will get the September National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) report, a detailed tracking of price, inventory and employment trends in the manufacturing sector.
"We do have a week of pretty important economic news in front of us that could affect the director or tone of things going forward," said Feinman.
For the first time in months, economists are forecasting more subdued payroll growth for September.

"The market jumped immediately after the GDP came out even though the revisions were penny-ante," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc. "Then a little after the Michigan consumer sentiment numbers came out, the market dropped like a stone. Prices then eroded very, very slowly and modestly for the rest of the day. In the end, it was probably nothing more than a little bit of profit-taking," he said.

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities, said a large volume of central bank buying helped the bond market earlier this week and the apparent lack of those purchases on Friday "perhaps led to a small retreat."

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that non-farm payrolls grew by 166,000 jobs in September, down from 250,000 in August. The economists said they expected the unemployment rate to tick up to 5.2 percent from 5.1 percent in August. Average hourly earnings are expected to be up 0.2 percent and the length of the average workweek is expected to edge up very slightly to 34.5 hours.
"Payrolls may be held down by some special factors, but when you put it in context, we've still got a very strong labor market," said Feinman.

Prices did not react to the Federal Reserve's release of the minutes from its August 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting. Those minutes disclosed that once again, Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern was the only Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) member who, dissenting from the majority, voted for a "modestly more restrictive" credit policy. At the meeting, members debated whether a jobless rate around 5.4 percent would lead to higher wages. And the policymakers emphasized their commitment to pre-empt actual inflation.
At the close, three-month bill rates were up two basis points to 4.90 percent. Six-month bill rates were down two basis points to 5.03 percent. Year bill rates rose two basis points to 5.36 percent.

Prices of the two-year notes slipped 1/32 to 99-28/32, yielding 6.07 percent. Five-year notes slipped 1/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 6.43 percent and the 10-year note fell 4/32 to 102-9/32 to yield 6.68 percent.
